newsitem.title: USA: Texas Instruments spin-off seen positive.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments spin-off seen positive.

text.p: A decision by Texas Instruments Inc to auction off its defense-electronics business would allow the semiconductor company to focus on its high-growth businesses, analysts said Wednesday.

Shrugging off concerns that a spin-off might make Texas Instruments even more vulnerable to volatility in the market for memory chips, its core product, industry experts said such a move would be a good one.

"Resources are being taken away from a low-growth business and put into a high-growth business. It will be volatile, but it means higher growth in the long term," said Drew Peck, an analyst with Cowen and Co.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Texas Instruments had made an initial call for bids for its defense-electronics division, hoping to get $2 billion or more for it.
Analysts said the timing appeared to be right.

"Prices are obviously high for companies in that segment, and it is a good time for TI to realize value for that business," said Mark Biagetti, a vice president at First Equity. "I think we are at the top of the market in that business."
In August, Boeing Co said it would buy Rockwell International Corp's aerospace and defence business for $3 billion.
Biagetti said a price tag of $2 billion or more for Texas Instruments' defense division, which generated $1.7 billion of revenues in 1995, would be in line with the Boeing-Rockwell deal.
Peck said a sale would have little or no immediate impact on earnings but would allow Texas Instruments to expand further.
"I fully expect them to be making significant acquisitions because they'll be sitting on a lot of cash," he said.
The defense-electronics division accounted for about 30 percent of total revenues in the late 1980s. That share had withered to less than 15 percent last year.

The unit makes advanced aircraft radar and infrared night-vision systems as well as high-technology "smart" missiles used during the Persian Gulf War in 1991. But the industry has come under pressure as the number of defense projects has shrunk.
